claim: Using measures of research productivity to assess academic performance puts women at a disadvantage because gender roles and unconscious biases, operating both at home and in academia, can affect research productivity.
source: Using measures of research productivity to assess academic performance puts women at a disadvantage because gender roles and unconscious biases, operating both at home and in academia, can affect research productivity.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus about gender bias in academia.

claim: The gender gap in research productivity increased during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: We find that the gender gap in research productivity increased during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the largest changes occurring in the social sciences and medicine, and the changes in the biological sciences and TEMCP (technology, engineering, mathematics, chemistry and physics) being much smaller.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis of 55 studies and 130 effect sizes presented in the manuscript.

claim: The largest changes in the gender gap during the pandemic occurred in the social sciences and medicine.
source: We find that the gender gap in research productivity increased during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the largest changes occurring in the social sciences and medicine, and the changes in the biological sciences and TEMCP (technology, engineering, mathematics, chemistry and physics) being much smaller.
evidence: This is supported by the meta-analysis results comparing different research fields.

claim: Women are disadvantaged compared to men when success is measured using traditional metrics of research productivity.
source: Women are disadvantaged compared to men when success is measured using traditional metrics of research productivity (Astegiano et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020), despite no actual differences in contribution and impact of research (van den Besselaar and Sandström, 2016; van den Besselaar and Sandström, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: There are no actual differences in contribution and impact of research between women and men.
source: Women are disadvantaged compared to men when success is measured using traditional metrics of research productivity (Astegiano et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020), despite no actual differences in contribution and impact of research (van den Besselaar and Sandström, 2016; van den Besselaar and Sandström, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Novel living and working conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic worsened the research productivity of many women worldwide.
source: Additionally, during the COVID-19 pandemic, novel living and working conditions worsened the research productivity of many women worldwide (Anwer, 2020; Boncori, 2020; Guy and Arthur, 2020; Herman et al., 2021; Altan‐Olcay and Bergeron, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Women generally perform more unpaid caregiving and domestic work.
source: First, women generally perform more unpaid caregiving and domestic work (Schiebinger et al., 2008; Schiebinger and Gilmartin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Social-distancing and facility closures during the pandemic increased caregiving and domestic work.
source: Social-distancing and facility closures during the pandemic increased caregiving and domestic work (Carli, 2020; Carlson et al., 2020) with reduced community help from nurseries, schools, care homes, house cleaners, laundrettes, nannies, babysitters and family (Myers et al., 2020; Barber et al., 2021; Breuning et al., 2021; Deryugina et al., 2021; Shalaby et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Women undertake more 'non-promotable' tasks such as administrative, supportive and mentoring roles.
source: Women undertake more 'non-promotable' tasks (Babcock et al., 2022) such as administrative, supportive and mentoring roles (Porter, 2007; Mitchell and Hesli, 2013; Babcock et al., 2017; Guarino and Borden, 2017; O'Meara et al., 2017a; O'Meara et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Changes in teaching and administration in response to the pandemic were more likely to be facilitated by women.
source: Changes in teaching and administration in response to the pandemic were therefore more likely to be facilitated by women (Docka‐Filipek and Stone, 2021; Minello et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Women generally perform more technical work such as generating data, whilst men assume more core tasks in conceptualisation, analysis, writing and publishing.
source: Women generally perform more technical work such as generating data, whilst men assume more core tasks in conceptualisation, analysis, writing and publishing (Macaluso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The surge in publications during the pandemic could have reduced the quality of peer review.
source: Additionally, the surge in publications during the pandemic (Else, 2020) could have reduced the quality of peer review, with evaluation being more influenced by cognitive shortcuts.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the surge in publications.

claim: Cognitive shortcuts in peer review are often associated with biases tending to operate against women.
source: These shortcuts are often associated with biases tending to operate against women (Kaatz et al., 2014; Reuben et al., 2014; Carli, 2020) resulting in lower success getting submissions accepted (Fox and Paine, 2019; Murray et al., 2019; Day et al., 2020; Hagan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The relative productivity of women to men decreased during the pandemic by –0.071 compared to before the pandemic.
source: Across the full dataset (N=130), after controlling for multiple effect sizes from the same study, we found the relative productivity of women to men decreased during the pandemic by –0.071 compared to before the pandemic (95% CI=−0.099 to −0.043, SE = 0.0144, p <0.001; Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the meta-analysis results and Figure 1.

claim: The relative productivity of women compared to men is 7% lower than what it was prior to the pandemic.
source: This indicates that the relative productivity of women compared to men is 7% lower than what it was prior to the pandemic, meaning that in cases where men and women were estimated to be equally productive, the productivity of women now is only 93% that of men.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the effect size of -0.071 from the meta-analysis.

claim: 38 effect sizes indicate a clear increase in the gender gap with 95% confidence intervals within negative ranges.
source: There is large variation in the 130 effect sizes, with 38 indicating a clear increase in the gender gap (95% confidence intervals within negative ranges) and 56 a trend of an increase (effect size is negative but 95% confidence intervals are not within negative ranges), while 11 indicate a clear decrease in the gender gap (95% confidence intervals within positive ranges) and 25 a trend of a decrease (effect size is positive but 95% confidence intervals are not within positive ranges).
evidence: This is a descriptive summary of the effect sizes in the dataset.

claim: Total heterogeneity was high (I2= 97.9%).
source: Total heterogeneity was high (I2= 97.9%), with 46.6% of it explained by whether research productivity was measured by survey responses or submission/publication numbers and 52.1% explained by the individual effect sizes.
evidence: This is a statistical measure from the meta-analysis.

claim: The degree of increase in the gender gap caused by the pandemic differed according to the type of research productivity measured.
source: The degree of increase in the gender gap caused by the pandemic differed according to the type of research productivity measured (QM (df = 3)=37.130, P<0.001; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical test and Figure 2.

claim: Studies measuring changes to research productivity during the pandemic based on surveys detected a larger overall effect (–0.192) than studies that compared the number of articles published (–0.047) or submitted (–0.053).
source: Studies measuring changes to research productivity during the pandemic based on surveys detected a larger overall effect (–0.192, 95% CI=−0.272 to −0.113, SE = 0.041, P<0.001) than studies that compared the number of articles published (–0.047, 95% CI=−0.085 to −0.008, P=0.017, SE = 0.020) or submitted (–0.053, 95% CI=−0.087 to −0.018, P=0.003, SE = 0.017) by authors of each gender before and during the pandemic.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results comparing different measurement types.

claim: Social sciences showed the greatest increases in the academic productivity gender gap during the pandemic (–0.084).
source: When considering research fields individually, social sciences showed the greatest increases in the academic productivity gender gap during the pandemic (–0.084, 95% CI=−0.143 to –0.024, SE = 0.030, P=0.006), followed by medicine (–0.066, 95% CI=−0.102 to –0.029, SE = 0.019, P<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results for different research fields.

claim: Medicine showed the second greatest increase in the academic productivity gender gap during the pandemic (–0.066).
source: When considering research fields individually, social sciences showed the greatest increases in the academic productivity gender gap during the pandemic (–0.084, 95% CI=−0.143 to –0.024, SE = 0.030, P=0.006), followed by medicine (–0.066, 95% CI=−0.102 to –0.029, SE = 0.019, P<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results for different research fields.

claim: The pandemic showed little effect in multidisciplinary fields (–0.050).
source: The pandemic showed little effect in multidisciplinary fields (–0.050, 95% CI=−0.125 to 0.024, SE = 0.038, P=0.188), biological sciences (–0.003, 95% CI=−0.057 to 0.050, SE = 0.027, P=0.902), or technology, engineering, mathematics, chemistry and physics (–0.003, 95% CI=−0.053 to 0.048, SE = 0.026, P=0.916).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results showing non-significant effects in these fields.

claim: The pandemic showed little effect in biological sciences (–0.003).
source: The pandemic showed little effect in multidisciplinary fields (–0.050, 95% CI=−0.125 to 0.024, SE = 0.038, P=0.188), biological sciences (–0.003, 95% CI=−0.057 to 0.050, SE = 0.027, P=0.902), or technology, engineering, mathematics, chemistry and physics (–0.003, 95% CI=−0.053 to 0.048, SE = 0.026, P=0.916).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results showing non-significant effects in these fields.

claim: The pandemic showed little effect in technology, engineering, mathematics, chemistry and physics (–0.003).
source: The pandemic showed little effect in multidisciplinary fields (–0.050, 95% CI=−0.125 to 0.024, SE = 0.038, P=0.188), biological sciences (–0.003, 95% CI=−0.057 to 0.050, SE = 0.027, P=0.902), or technology, engineering, mathematics, chemistry and physics (–0.003, 95% CI=−0.053 to 0.048, SE = 0.026, P=0.916).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results showing non-significant effects in these fields.

claim: The pandemic has increased the gender gap in article output more in journals/repositories/pre-print servers that were previously less gender-disparate.
source: Based on this subset of data, we found that the pandemic has increased the gender gap in article output more in journals/repositories/pre-print servers that were previously less gender-disparate (QM(df = 1)=10.285, P=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-regression analysis.

claim: Fields with a smaller gender gap prior to the pandemic experienced greater gender disparity in academic productivity during the pandemic compared with fields where the gender gap was already large.
source: When grouping studies by research fields (Figure 4), those with a smaller gender gap prior to the pandemic experienced greater gender disparity in academic productivity during the pandemic compared with fields where the gender gap was already large to start with (Social sciences: 35.8% to 33.4%, medicine: 36.6% to 33.8%, multidisciplinary: 36.2% to 34.2%, biological sciences: 32.7% to 32.7%, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics, Chemistry and Physics: 23.0% to 22.1%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The pandemic had a significant effect on first authorship roles (–0.040).
source: The pandemic had a significant effect on first authorship roles (–0.040, 95% CI=−0.073 to –0.007, SE = 0.017, P=0.019) but not for all authorship roles (–0.045, 95% CI=−0.107 to 0.017, SE = 0.320, P=0.154), corresponding authorship roles (–0.058, 95% CI=−0.123 to 0.007, SE = 0.033, P=0.080), middle authorship roles (–0.045, 95% CI=−0.173 to 0.820, SE = 0.065, P=0.485) or last authorship roles (–0.040, 95% CI=−0.094 to 0.015, SE = 0.028, P=0.152).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results for different authorship positions.

claim: The multilevel meta-regression showed no evidence of publication bias.
source: The multilevel meta-regression, including article studies and survey studies as a moderator because of their differences in sample size, showed no evidence of publication bias (article studies: slope = –0.025, 95% CI=−0.059 to −0.009, SE = 0.017, P=0.148; survey studies: slope = –0.157, 95% CI=−0.244 to −0.071, SE = 0.044, P<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the publication bias analysis.

claim: A visual inspection of the funnel plots did not indicate any suggestion of publication bias.
source: A visual inspection of the funnel plots similarly did not indicate any suggestion of publication bias (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of Figure 6.

claim: When excluding seven effect sizes using four measures of productivity from survey studies that are less directly comparable, the overall estimate was –0.063.
source: When excluding these effect sizes, the overall estimate was –0.063 (95% CI=−0.0892 to −0.0372, SE = 0.0133, P<0.001), and the estimate for survey studies only was –0.239 (95% CI=−0.3419 to −0.1352, SE = 0.0527, P<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated gender gaps in academic productivity.
source: Our study finds quantitative evidence, based on 55 studies and 130 effect sizes, to support the hypothesis that the COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated gender gaps in academic productivity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the meta-analysis.

claim: Gender gaps in research productivity within academia increased on average by 7% relative to the gender gaps that existed before the pandemic.
source: Overall, the studies summarised in our meta-analysis suggest that gender gaps in research productivity within academia increased on average by 7% relative to the gender gaps that existed before the pandemic.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the meta-analysis.

claim: When measuring research productivity as the number of published or submitted articles, the increase in the gap is around 5%.
source: When measuring research productivity as the number of published or submitted articles, we find a slightly smaller increase in the gap of around 5%.
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis results for article studies.

claim: The proportion of authors on submitted or published articles who are women declined from an average of 33.2% pre-pandemic to 31.4% during the pandemic.
source: This corresponds to the proportion of authors on submitted or published articles who are women declining from an average of 33.2% pre-pandemic to 31.4% during the pandemic (–0.05 * 33.2%=–1.7%).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the effect size for article studies.

claim: When measured by surveys, productivity reduction was 19% higher than in men.
source: When measured by surveys, productivity reduction was 19% higher than in men.
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis results for survey studies.

claim: The study likely underestimates the pandemic effect on article productivity in women because writing and publishing can take a long time.
source: Our study likely underestimates the pandemic effect on article productivity in women because writing and publishing can take a long time (Powell, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference about publication timelines.

claim: Many of the articles submitted or published during the pandemic were likely started and at least partially completed prior to the pandemic.
source: Many of the articles submitted or published during the pandemic were likely started and at least partially completed prior to the pandemic, given that most research grants span multiple years.
evidence: This is an inference based on typical research timelines.

claim: Most of the studies in the sample obtained their data relatively soon after when the WHO officially declared a pandemic (median of 7 months after January 2020).
source: Most of the studies in our sample obtained their data relatively soon after when the WHO officially declared a pandemic (median of 7 months after January 2020).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the studies included in the meta-analysis.

claim: Five of six survey studies report evidence of a negative interaction effect of being both female and a parent on research productivity during the pandemic.
source: In the literature used within our meta-analysis, five of six survey studies report evidence of a negative interaction effect of being both female and a parent on research productivity during the pandemic, presumably because of increased caregiving demands.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the survey studies included in the meta-analysis.

claim: The pandemic may have differentially impacted female researchers across research fields, with increases in gender gaps particularly visible in research fields that were nearest to being gender-equal before the pandemic.
source: Our analysis suggests the pandemic may have differentially impacted female researchers across research fields, with increases in gender gaps particularly visible in research fields that were nearest to being gender-equal before the pandemic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the meta-analysis results.

claim: Social sciences and medicine were two fields closest to gender equality that experienced the most significant decrease in female authors.
source: Social sciences and medicine were two fields closest to gender equality that experienced the most significant decrease in female authors.
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis results for different research fields.

claim: Many medical journals sped up the publication process during the pandemic.
source: Additionally, many medical journals sped up the publication process (Horbach, 2020), so the real-time effect of the pandemic on research productivity in women versus men may be reflected more in papers submitted and published in medicine than in other fields.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The pandemic increased the gender gap particularly among first authors.
source: We found that the pandemic increased the gender gap particularly among first authors, potentially suggesting that women were particularly more restricted in the time they had available to write papers.
evidence: This is based on the meta-analysis results for authorship positions, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: It seems unlikely that this change in the gender gap during the pandemic simply represents a normal temporal fluctuation.
source: It seems unlikely that this change in the gender gap during the pandemic simply represents a normal temporal fluctuation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the magnitude of the effect and comparison to historical trends.

claim: A study comparing the change in the proportion of female authors between 1945 and 2005 showed a steady increase from 14% of all authors being women to 35%, with no apparent year-on-year decline since at least 1990.
source: This decline is steep relative to a study comparing the change in the proportion of female authors between 1945 and 2005 that showed a steady increase from 14% of all authors being women to 35%, with no apparent year-on-year decline since at least 1990 (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The systematic literature review identified 55 studies that met the inclusion criteria.
source: Our systematic literature review identified 55 studies that met the inclusion criteria (for details on the procedure please see the Methods section).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology and results of the literature search.

claim: All of the identified studies only compared women to men.
source: All of the identified studies only compared women to men (see Limitations).
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the included studies.

claim: 130 effect sizes were extracted and calculated from the 55 studies.
source: We extracted and calculated 130 effect sizes from these studies and performed a meta-analysis and meta-regression to test our three hypotheses and related predictions.
evidence: This is a description of the data extraction process.

claim: Out of 130 effect sizes, 23 are based on survey responses and 107 are studies that measure the number of submitted or published articles.
source: Out of 130 effect sizes, 23 are based on survey responses (survey studies), and 107 are studies that measure the number of submitted or published articles (article studies).
evidence: This is a description of the composition of the dataset.

claim: There was little evidence of a significant differential impact of research fields on the reported effect sizes.
source: For effect sizes from article studies grouped by research field (N=107), we found little evidence of a significant differential impact of research fields on the reported effect sizes (QM (df = 5)=21.967, P=0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on the statistical test, though the p-value suggests significance.

claim: There was no evidence of a significant differential impact of authorship position on effect sizes.
source: Based on these data, we found no evidence of a significant differential impact of authorship position on effect sizes (QM(df = 5)=13.190, P=0.022; Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the statistical test, though the p-value suggests significance.

claim: The scoping search identified 21 original research publications with quantitative metrics investigating differences in academic productivity by gender before and during the pandemic.
source: The scoping search identified 21 original research publications with quantitative metrics investigating differences in academic productivity by gender before and during the pandemic (Supplementary file 1, "Scoping search" sheet).
evidence: This is a description of the scoping search results.

claim: Of the 21 scoped texts, 14 were indexed by Web of Science, and 17 were indexed by Scopus.
source: Of these 21 studies (scoped texts), 14 were indexed by Web of Science, and 17 (including the same 14 from Web of Science) were indexed by Scopus.
evidence: This is a description of the database coverage of the scoped texts.

claim: The initial search in Scopus generated 722 texts, including 13/17 (76.5%) of scoped texts indexed by Scopus.
source: The initial search in Scopus generated 722 texts, including 13/17 (76.5%) of scoped texts indexed by Scopus.
evidence: This is a description of the initial search results.

claim: The refined search was performed on 27/07/2021 and generated 700 total texts combined from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO, and Proquest from 2020 onwards.
source: We performed the refined search on 27/07/2021 and generated 700 total texts combined from Scopus (126 texts, including 13/17 studies found in the scoping search), the Web of Science core collection (199 texts), EBSCO (276 texts and Proquest (99 texts)) from 2020 onwards.
evidence: This is a description of the refined search process and results.

claim: The final search hit rate had an efficiency of 10.3% (13/126) on Scopus.
source: The final search hit rate had an efficiency of 10.3% (13/126) on Scopus.
evidence: This is a description of the search efficiency.

claim: After removing duplicates, 580 texts remained to enter the study screening stage.
source: After removing duplicates, 580 texts remained to enter the study screening stage.
evidence: This is a description of the screening process.

claim: The agreement rate between reviewers was 97%, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.86.
source: The agreement rate between reviewers was 97%, with 49 studies that both authors agreed to include, 357 studies which both excluded, ten studies one reviewer included but the other excluded, and four studies only included by the other reviewer. This agreement rate resulted in a, "strong" (McHugh, 2012) to "near perfect" (Landis and Koch, 1977) Cohen's kappa of 0.86.
evidence: This is a description of the inter-rater reliability in the screening process.

claim: Out of the 580 texts, 70 were retained for the full text screening.
source: Overall, out of the 580 texts, 70 were retained for the full text screening (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a description of the screening results.

claim: 25 studies that all contained necessary metrics to calculate effect sizes were retained for data extraction, excluding 45 studies.
source: Thus, 25 studies that all contained necessary metrics to calculate effect sizes were retained for data extraction, excluding 45 studies (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a description of the full-text screening results.

claim: The second search was repeated on 28/02/2022, generating 1646 total texts combined from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO, and Proquest from 2020 onwards.
source: The second search was repeated on 28/02/2022, generating 1646 total texts combined from Scopus (258 texts, including 14/17 studies found in the scoping search), the Web of Science core collection (413 texts), EBSCO (542 texts) and Proquest (433 texts) from 2020 onwards.
evidence: This is a description of the iterated search process.

claim: 438 duplicates were removed using Rayyan.ai, leaving 1208 de-duplicated studies.
source: We removed 438 duplicates using Rayyan.ai, leaving 1208 de-duplicated studies.
evidence: This is a description of the duplicate removal process.

claim: Out of the 1208 texts from the final search, 170 were included after screening titles, abstracts and keywords.
source: Out of the 1208 texts from the final search, we included 170 after screening titles, abstracts and keywords.
evidence: This is a description of the screening results.

claim: For the 169 texts, full texts were screened, excluding 120 studies and keeping 50 that all contained the necessary information to calculate the effect sizes.
source: For these 169, we screened the full texts, excluding 120 studies (53 studies missed one qualifier, 38 studies missed two qualifiers, 27 studies miss three qualifiers, 1 study missed four qualifiers) and keeping 50 (including the 25 identified in the original search) that all contained the necessary information to calculate the effect sizes (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a description of the full-text screening results.

claim: Five studies found in the scoping search but not returned in database searches were also included, resulting in 55 total studies used to extract variables for analysis.
source: Five studies found in the scoping search but not returned in database searches were also included, resulting in 55 total studies used to extract variables for analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample of studies.

claim: The sample consists of 130 effect sizes obtained from 55 studies including surveys of potentially affected people and comparisons of numbers of articles submitted or published by gender before and during the pandemic.
source: Our sample consists of 130 effect sizes obtained from 55 studies including surveys of potentially affected people (Myers et al., 2020; Rodríguez-Rivero et al., 2020; Barber et al., 2021; Breuning et al., 2021; Camerlink et al., 2021; Candido, 2021; Deryugina et al., 2021; Ovalle Diaz et al., 2021; Ellinas et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2021; Ghaffarizadeh et al., 2021; Guintivano et al., 2021; Hoggarth et al., 2021; Krukowski et al., 2021; Maguire et al., 2021; Plaunova et al., 2021; Shalaby et al., 2021; Staniscuaski et al., 2021; Yildirim and Eslen-Ziya, 2021; Davis et al., 2022; Stenson et al., 2022), and comparisons of numbers of articles submitted or published by gender before and during the pandemic (Amano-Patiño, 2020; Andersen et al., 2020; Bell and Green, 2020; Cushman, 2020; Inno et al., 2020; Kibbe, 2020; Vincent-Lamarre et al., 2020; Wehner et al., 2020; Bell and Fong, 2021; Biondi et al., 2021; Cook et al., 2021; DeFilippis et al., 2021; Forti et al., 2021; Fox and Meyer, 2021; Gayet-Ageron et al., 2021; Gerding et al., 2021; Ipe et al., 2021; Jemielniak et al., 2021; Jordan and Carlezon, 2021; King and Frederickson, 2021; Lerchenmüller et al., 2021; Mogensen et al., 2021; Muric et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2021; Quak et al., 2021; Ribarovska et al., 2021; Squazzoni et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2021; Anabaraonye et al., 2022; Ayyala and Trout, 2022; Chen and Seto, 2022; Cui et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2022; Wooden and Hanson, 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the final sample with citations to all included studies.

claim: For 10 effect sizes which did not have data available to calculate effect sizes, already calculated percentage changes in the gender gap were used.
source: For 10 effect sizes which did not have data available to calculate our own effect sizes, we used already calculated percentage changes in the gender gap in academic productivity as predicted from lasso regression (N=2), Somers' delta (N=2), ordered logistic regression (N=1) and mixed-effect models (N=5).
evidence: This is a description of the effect size calculation methodology.

claim: For 120 effect sizes, summary data or simple statistical tests were entered into Campbell collaboration's effect size calculator to calculate a standardised mean difference (d) effect size.
source: For 120 effect sizes, we entered summary data (N=117) or simple statistical tests (N=3) into Campbell collaboration's effect size calculator (Wilson, 2019) to calculate a standardised mean difference (d) effect size.
evidence: This is a description of the effect size calculation methodology.

claim: 10 effect sizes were calculated by obtaining raw numbers from graphs, estimated using Adobe Acrobat's measure tool.
source: 10 effect sizes were calculated by obtaining raw numbers from graphs, estimated using Adobe Acrobat's measure tool (Supplementary file 1, "Calculations" sheet).
evidence: This is a description of the data extraction methodology.

claim: Two effect sizes were calculated using sample sizes obtained by personal correspondence with the article authors.
source: Two effect sizes (Jemielniak et al., 2021; Stenson et al., 2022) were calculated using sample sizes obtained by personal correspondence with the article authors.
evidence: This is a description of the data extraction methodology.

claim: Academic institutions should acknowledge and carefully accommodate the pandemic period when using research productivity to evaluate female academics for career progression in the coming years.
source: Academic institutions should acknowledge and carefully accommodate the pandemic period when using research productivity to evaluate female academics for career progression in the coming years.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Tenure-clock extensions designed to accommodate pandemic disruption may inadvertently exacerbate the gender gap by extending the period that advantaged individuals can outperform.
source: For example, tenure-clock extensions designed to accommodate pandemic disruption may inadvertently exacerbate the gender gap by extending the period that advantaged individuals can outperform.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential unintended consequences of interventions.

claim: More emphasis must be placed evaluating academic merit using more holistic measures and on an individual basis.
source: More emphasis must be placed evaluating academic merit using more holistic measures and on an individual basis.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The study cannot speak to the potential mechanisms that might have led to changes in gender inequality during the pandemic.
source: Our study cannot speak to the potential mechanisms that might have led to changes in gender inequality during the pandemic and is therefore limited in deriving suggestions for potential interventions to potentially ameliorate unfair differential productivity besides indicating that such inequalities appear pervasive.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Gender is investigated only as a binary variable, mostly using first-name prediction tools, with no investigation into non-binary or transgender.
source: Gender is investigated only as a binary variable, mostly using first-name prediction tools, with no investigation into non-binary or transgender.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the included studies.

claim: Studies using numbers of submissions or publications to measure research productivity used automatic approaches that are more likely to mis-gender individuals as they inferred binary gender based on first names.
source: In addition, studies using numbers of submissions or publications (38 out of 55) to measure research productivity used automatic approaches that are more likely to mis-gender individuals as they inferred binary gender based on first names.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the included studies.

claim: Automatic gender inference approaches are often restricted to names common in English speaking countries.
source: While these approaches seemingly offer the potential to identify trends in larger samples, they themselves introduce and reinforce biases in relation to gender that are hard to assess, intersecting with biases in ethnicity as these approaches are often restricted to names common in English speaking countries (Mihaljević et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most studies explored academic populations worldwide (N=99 effect sizes), or from Western (N=28 effect sizes) regions, but not the Global South (N=3 effect sizes).
source: Most studies explored academic populations worldwide (N=99 effect sizes), or from Western (N=28 effect sizes) regions, but not the Global South (N=3 effect sizes) limiting investigation of interaction effects between geographic regions.
evidence: This is a description of the geographic distribution of the studies.

claim: Conclusions from survey studies are limited to North American and Western European, since 18/23 studies are exclusive to or have the majority of respondents from these regions.
